chunks.text: How-to · June 7, twenty twenty-six · 6 min read · By Don Goldstein

Ground beef is at a record near 6.90 dollars a pound and food-away-from-home prices are forecast up 3.6% this year. The move is not to raise the whole menu — it is to find the few plates that actually moved and re-cost those.
In short
Ground beef hit a record near 6.90 dollars/lb (BLS, April twenty twenty-six) and the USDA forecasts food-away-from-home prices up 3.6% for twenty twenty-six.
Do not raise the whole menu — re-cost the three to five plates whose inputs actually moved, and pick the lever per plate.
Price into a cautious diner: the NRA found 85% pulling back on spending, but 61% still call dining out essential.

Ground beef crossed a record this spring — about 6.90 dollars a pound in April — and the USDA expects food-away-from-home prices up 3.6% across twenty twenty-six. Coffee, oils, and eggs have moved too. The reflex is to raise the whole menu. Don’t. The whole menu didn’t move; three to five plates did. Re-cost those.

A menu-wide raise is the expensive shortcut. It punishes the items that are still fine, it reads as greed to a diner who is already watching the check, and it doesn’t actually fix the plates bleeding margin — it hides them in an average.
Re-cost the five that moved.

Re-costing the plates that moved, in four steps. One: find the moved inputs — beef, eggs, oils, coffee — and pull the three to five plates whose main input jumped, not the whole menu. Two: re-cost each recipe card; the plate cost shows the new food cost and contribution margin. Three: pick the lever per plate — raise, re-portion, or re-engineer, item by item, not across the board. Four: hold the rest — leave the unaffected items alone, because a menu-wide raise reads as greed and hides the real problem in an average.
Price into a cautious diner.

The timing is the hard part, because the twenty twenty-six diner is watching the check. The National Restaurant Association found 85% of consumers pulling back on spending this year — and, at the same time, 61% saying dining out is essential to how they live. Both are true. They will still come; they will also notice a clumsy raise. So move the price where the value is obvious — the signature plate, the one with the best photo and description — and protect the average check rather than chasing it.

The twenty twenty-six diner, by the numbers, from the National Restaurant Association. Eighty-five percent of consumers are pulling back on spending. At the same time, sixty-one percent say dining out is essential to how they live. Both are true at once — diners are cautious but committed.
The other input that moved.

If you’re in DC, labor moved too — the July 1 wage step stacks on top of food cost. Re-cost and re-price once, for both, rather than twice. Track it going forward with cost pulse so the next spike shows up in a week, not a quarter, and the full pricing playbook is in raising prices without losing reservations .
Re-cost the five that moved. Hold the rest. That is the whole move.
Key takeaways
A menu-wide raise punishes the items that are fine and hides the real problem in an average.
Re-cost the moved plates with a recipe-cost card; the plate cost shows the new contribution margin.
Move the price where the value is obvious — the signature plate — and protect the average check.
In DC, the July 1 wage step stacks on food cost; re-cost and re-price once for both.
